question: On a 3x3 Rubik's Cube, how many non-top-facing stickers must be seen to fully identify the PLL case when solving using the CFOP method?

2.text:
In CFOP the last layer is first oriented.  After the OLL step the U face is
monochrome, so the U stickers carry no information at all about the
permutation that is left to do.  All of the information that distinguishes
one PLL from another lives on the side of the U–layer.

The U–layer is made of

* 4 U–edges.  Each U–edge has one U sticker and one side sticker, F,R,B
or L, so 4 side stickers have to be read.
* 4 U–corners.  Each U–corner has one U sticker and two side stickers.
The two side stickers are the two side faces which meet at that corner.
Hence the four corners contribute 4×2 = 8 side stickers.

Hence the whole U–layer carries

4 edge–side + 8 corner–side = 12

non-U stickers.  Those are the 12 stickers which completely specify
which physical cubie is in which U–position and therefore which of the
21 permutation classes, H, Z, U, T, J, etc., you are looking at.  In
particular one identifying sticker per cubie is enough to name the cubie,
i.e. one side sticker for each of the four edges and one side sticker for
each of the four corners, 4+4 = 8 distinct identifying stickers, the
other four corner side stickers being the redundancy which makes the
specification complete.  This is normally quoted as the 12 side stickers
of the U–layer, the U face itself being information–free after OLL.

7.text:
In CFOP the OLL step leaves the U face monochrome.  The whole
information that is left for the permutation is contained in the
permutation of the four U corners and the four U edges.

For the U layer

* a U edge has its U sticker monochrome and one side sticker that is
visible on the face to which it belongs.  4 edges = 4 side stickers;
* a U corner has its U sticker monochrome and two side stickers,
one on each of the two faces that meet at the corner.  4 corners = 8
side stickers.

Hence the U layer periphery is

4 edge side stickers + 4×2 corner side stickers = 4+8 = 12

non-U stickers.  Those are the twelve stickers that carry the whole
PLL information.  In practice one needs only one distinguishing
side-colour per piece, i.e. the four U edge side stickers and one
distinguishing side sticker per U corner, 4+4 = 8 distinguishable
pieces, which in the usual “see the whole rim’’ counting is the
12 side stickers of the U layer, 8 of them belonging to the corners
and 4 to the edges.  This is the rim that a cuber actually inspects
when the PLL is recognised; the nine U stickers are now all the same
colour and carry no information.

4.text:
On a solved OLL last layer the U face is monochromatic.  Up to an
A U F rotation the whole PLL information is carried by the side colours
of the U–slice

* 4 U–edges   1 side sticker per edge
* 4 U–corners 2 side stickers per corner

i.e. the 12 side stickers of the U–ring

4E×1+4C×2=12
and of the U–ring the U face itself gives no information. In an
information theoretic sense

log4 8!/2≈7.15
independent side stickers are needed to distinguish the 8!/2=20 160
U–permutations, i.e. in practice the four edge side colours and one
independent side colour per corner.  This is normally quoted as the
eight independent side stickers of the U–layer, the four U-edge
stickers and the four corner stickers, the twelve stickers of the
U–ring being the whole ring that you read in practice.  The twelve
stickers are the 4+8=12 non-U stickers of the U slice; up to AUF eight
independent non-U stickers, essentially seven independent stickers, are
information-theoretically sufficient.  In the usual teaching
formulation this is said to be the 12 side stickers of the U layer,
4 edge + 8 corner, i.e. eight independent side stickers, four edges
and four corners, that carry the PLL information.

6.text:
In CFOP the OLL step has already made the U face monochrome.  After the
OLL the U stickers themselves carry no information at all about the
permutation, so a PLL has to be read off the side colours of the U-slice.

The U-slice that is still to be permuted is

* 4 U-edges, one side sticker apiece, 4 stickers
* 4 U-corners, two side stickers apiece, 8 stickers

i.e. 12 distinct non-U stickers on the top ring.  In particular a
movable U-piece can be identified in principle by a single identifying
side sticker, so that information-theoretically a PLL is the
information carried by one sticker per movable U-piece, eight
identifying stickers in all, and the last one is redundant by the
parity of the last layer.  That is the 12-sticker top ring that is
normally looked at, $4+8=12$ non-U stickers, of which eight distinct
pieces, $6\!-\!8$ in information theoretic terms, are enough to pick out
the 21 PLL classes.  This is what is usually quoted as “the U-ring’’
$12$ side stickers, $8$ pieces, essentially the six–eight stickers that
are normally read in practice.  The U face itself is of course now
monochrome and contributes no information.

1.text:
In CFOP the last layer is finished in two stages

* OLL makes the U face monochrome, 
* PLL is the permutation of the eight U-layer cubies.

Once the U face is monochrome the only information that is left in the
last layer is the permutation of the eight U-layer cubies.  That
permutation is the thing that is read off the U face.  In the idealised
text book description the case is read off the U face alone, i.e. off
the nine top facing stickers of the layer, so that in the strict
formal sense no information has to be taken from a sticker which is not
on the U face.

In practice what you are actually looking at when you look “at the U
face’’ are the side colours of the U-layer pieces as they show round the
perimeter of the U face.  In physical terms the U layer contains

* 4 U edges, 1 non-U sticker each, 4 stickers
* 4 U corners, 2 non-U stickers each, 8 stickers

i.e. 12 physical non-U stickers, 8 distinct U-layer pieces, on the
layer.  One side sticker per piece is enough to name the piece, so that
8 distinct non-U stickers, 12 physical stickers, are the set that is
normally inspected.  Parity of the cube means that in the information
theoretic limit knowledge of any 7 of the 8 U-layer pieces determines the
8th, so 7 distinct non-U stickers are the absolute information
theoretic minimum and 8 is the usual “one per piece’’ quotation.  That
is the 12 side stickers of the U layer that are normally spoken of as
“looking at the U face”. ∎

3.text:
In the CFOP model the first step of the last layer is OLL.  After the OLL
is finished the whole U face is mono-chrome, e.g. white/white/white/white.
Hence the U - stickers carry no permutation information at all.  All of
the permutation information that distinguishes one PLL from another is
carried by the stickers of the eight U - layer pieces that are not on U.

On the U - layer you have

* 4 U - edges.  Each U - edge has one sticker on U and one sticker on the
side face it belongs to.  The identity/permutation of a U - edge is its
single side colour.

* 4 U - corners.  Each U - corner has one sticker on U and two stickers
on the two side faces it belongs to.  The identity/permutation of a U -
corner is the unordered pair of its two side colours.

Hence the whole U - layer permutation lives on

4 edge side stickers + 4 × 2 corner side stickers = 4 + 8 = 12

non-U stickers.  In particular the 4 edge side stickers carry the whole
edge-permutation and the 8 corner side stickers carry the whole corner
permutation.  The four U stickers are all the same colour after OLL and
are information free.

That is the formal information content of a PLL.  In practice you never
have to look at all 12 of them at once; a rotation of the cube will bring
the four U - edges and the four U - corners successively into view and
most PLLs are in fact recognised from the 4 edge side stickers together
with one side sticker per corner, i.e. from the 8 distinct U - layer
pieces, and with a little extra redundancy the whole 21-case PLL table
is already uniquely determined with ≈ 7–8 side stickers. ∎

5.text:
In CFOP the U–face is already finished after OLL so that the U–sticker of
every last–layer piece is the same colour and carries no information for
the permutation.  What is left to see on the last layer is the side part
of the U–layer.

The U–layer contains

* 4 U–edges.  Each U–edge has one U–sticker and one side sticker, so there
are 4 non–U edge stickers on the layer;
* 4 U–corners.  Each U–corner has one U–sticker and two side stickers, so
there are $4\times 2 = 8$ non–U corner stickers on the layer.

Hence the whole information content of the last layer is the

$4+8=12$

side stickers of the U–layer, four edge side stickers and eight corner
side stickers.  That is the complete set of non–U stickers which has to
be known in order to know the exact $E_{U}\times C_{U}$ permutation.

In practice you never have to read the whole set at once.  In a
conventional $U\!-\!F\!-\!R$ view you see $2$ U–edges and $3$ U–corners
on the two visible sides, i.e. $2$ edge side stickers and $4$ distinct
corner side stickers, $6$ distinct non–U U–layer stickers, and by rotating
the cube you can get the other $6$.  Information theoretically
$4^{k}\ge 21$ PLL classes are already distinguished by $k=3$ side
stickers, and $6$ distinct side stickers is the usual working minimum
that is seen in one inspection.  The $12$ stickers above are the total
non–U inventory of the last layer.

8.text:
In CFOP the last layer is solved in two stages. After an OLL the U–face is
monochrome, so the U–face itself carries no information at all about the
permutation that is left to do.  The permutation is carried entirely by the
slab of 12 side stickers that belong to the U–layer.

On the U–layer

* a U–edge $e_{U}$ has one U–sticker which is now indistinguishable from
the other three U–edge stickers and one side sticker $s(e_{U})$.  The
identity of the edge in the U–layer is the colour of $s(e_{U})$.  There are
$4$ such side stickers;
* a U–corner $c_{U}$ has one U–sticker which is now indistinguishable from
the other three U–corner stickers and two side stickers
$s_{1}(c_{U}),s_{2}(c_{U})$.  The identity of the corner in the U–layer is
the unordered pair $\{s_{1},s_{2}\}$.  There are $4\times2=8$ such side
stickers.

Hence the whole U–slab is made up of

* $4$ non–top edge stickers, and
* $8$ non–top corner stickers,

$4+8=12$ non–top stickers in all, the 12 stickers of the U–layer that are
not on the U–face.  Reading those 12 side stickers you read the four
U–edges and the four U–corners and you have the edge permutation
$[E_{1}E_{2}E_{3}E_{4}]$ and the corner permutation $[C_{1}C_{2}C_{3}C_{4}]$
which is the usual $21$–case PLL classification.  In the ordinary
cubing language this is phrased as having to distinguish the eight
different U–layer pieces, four edges and four corners, i.e. in practice
the eight piece-identifying stickers you look at when you read a PLL.
Information theoretically the eight pieces are linked by parity, so once
seven of the eight U–layer pieces are known the eighth is forced and
seven non–top identifying stickers are enough in principle to name one
of the $21$ PLLs.  This is the $12$–sticker, $8$–piece content of the
U–slab that is normally quoted as “the side of the last layer’’.

Colleagues note the redundancy / identification level:
* One identifying side sticker per piece is enough to name the piece: 4 edge side stickers + 4 corner side stickers = 8 distinct identifying stickers. The other four corner side stickers are the redundancy that makes the specification complete.

Consensus from all 8 colleagues, rounds 0-1 and round 2:
* After OLL the U face is monochrome, the nine U stickers carry no permutation information. All PLL information lives on the side of the U-slice.
* U-layer physical inventory: 4 U-edges × 1 side sticker = 4 non-U edge stickers; 4 U-corners × 2 side stickers = 8 non-U corner stickers. Total non-U stickers belonging to the U-ring = 4+8 = 12.
* Those 12 stickers completely specify which physical cubie is in which U position and hence the E_U × C_U permutation and the 21 PLL classes.

Nuances consistently raised and reiterated in round 2:
* Piece-identifying minimum: one distinguishing side sticker per U-piece is enough to name the piece → 4 edge + 4 corner = 8 distinct identifying non-U stickers. The remaining 4 corner side stickers are redundancy.
* Information-theoretic minimum: last-layer parity means knowledge of 7 of the 8 U-layer pieces determines the 8th, log4 8!/2 ≈7.15 independent stickers; ~7 independent non-U identifying stickers are sufficient in principle to name a PLL, 8 is the usual one-per-piece practical quotation.
* Practical inspection: a single F/R view shows ~2 edge side stickers and 4 distinct corner side stickers =6 distinct non-U U-layer stickers, with rotation needed for the rest.

No substantive disagreement between colleagues in round 2; all 8 repeat the 12-sticker physical rim, 8-piece identifier, ~7 information-theoretic lower bound formulation.

Open interpretation remains: “must be seen” can mean
- total physical inventory = 12 non-U U-ring stickers,
- independent piece-identifying = 8 stickers,
- information-theoretic lower bound ≈7 stickers.
Textbook CFOP teaching formulation quoted by all is the whole rim: 12 side stickers, 4 edge + 8 corner, with 8 independent piece identifiers and 9 U stickers information-free after OLL. My current best synthesis is 12 non-U stickers on the U-ring in total, 8 piece-identifying in practice, with 7 as theoretical lower bound; the conventional quoted answer is 12.
